title: Working Capital Management
subtitle: Cash, inventory, receivables - the turnover cycle
openingQuestion: A business is profitable but still runs out of cash. Why?
openingOptions: Working capital is tied up: too much inventory, slow collections, fast payments to suppliers
explanation: Managing working capital means managing the cash trapped in day-to-day operations, and it has three levers: collect from customers faster, hold inventory for fewer days, pay suppliers more slowly. Every day shaved off frees up cash without needing to borrow. This is why fast-growing companies often run short of cash despite being profitable: as revenue rises, inventory and receivables rise with it, and they eat up cash before the cash comes back in.

realWorldExample.description: A manufacturer growing revenue 50% a year typically needs a matching increase in working capital (more raw materials, inventory, receivables) - if not managed tightly, the growth rate can outpace the ability to fund working capital, leading to a cash crunch even while the business remains profitable.

quiz.question: Which approach frees up working capital fastest?
options: Collect faster, reduce inventory, pay suppliers more slowly
Increase revenue, because higher revenue frees up working capital on its own
Increase profit, because profit is booked straight into the period's working capital
Borrow more from the bank, because loan cash turns working capital positive again
quiz.explanation: Cash Conversion Cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO. Cut DSO (invoice faster, offer discounts), cut DIO (JIT inventory), raise DPO (negotiate payment terms). Amazon has a negative CCC - customers pay before Amazon has to pay its suppliers.

quiz.question: Why can "growing too fast" sometimes be the very reason a business goes bankrupt, even while it shows a profit on paper?
options: Working capital has nothing to do with revenue growth rate
Growth needs more working capital; failing to raise it in time means running out of cash
Only a loss-making business carries bankruptcy risk, a profitable one does not
Fast growth never creates any financial risk for a company
quiz.explanation: This is the "growing broke" phenomenon mentioned in the Reading Financial Statements track: growth requires capital, and if a company has no plan to fund the working capital that growth demands, even a profitable business with a good model can run out of cash and go bankrupt.

quiz.question: Revenue grows 50% a year but the business runs out of cash. Why?
options: Because interest expense grows faster than the rate of revenue growth
Because margins always fall when revenue grows too fast
Because working capital must rise before the cash comes back in
Because taxes payable rise along with revenue in the same period
quiz.explanation: Growth requires buying more inventory, extending more credit to customers, holding a larger warehouse - all of which spend cash upfront. A business can be profitable on paper and still die from running out of cash, and the faster it grows, the more easily it dies.

quiz.question: What does negative working capital mean at a supermarket chain?
options: Short-term debt has been converted into long-term debt, a refinancing move unrelated to supplier terms
The business is losing the ability to meet short-term obligations
Inventory has been written down in value during the reporting period
Collecting from customers upfront and paying suppliers later
quiz.explanation: With a model that collects cash immediately and pays suppliers 30-60 days later, negative working capital is a sign of bargaining power rather than danger - the supplier is essentially providing free financing.

quiz.question: Which way of freeing up working capital does the least damage to relationships?
options: Shortening the time goods sit in inventory
Extending the payment term given to suppliers
Tightening credit limits for every customer
Cutting prices deeply so customers pay cash immediately
quiz.explanation: The three working capital levers aren't equal in cost: squeezing suppliers and tightening on customers both cost something in the relationship, while selling faster improves all three figures at once.

keyTakeaways: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Cash Conversion Cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO
A negative CCC (like Amazon's): customers pay first, suppliers get paid later - ideal

practicePrompt.question: A company wants to improve Working Capital Management to free up more cash for its operations. Which three actions below actually have a direct impact on the formula Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities?
options: Only increasing sales revenue affects Working Capital - the other factors are unrelated
Cut excess inventory, collect from customers faster, and stretch supplier payment terms sensibly
Only taking on more long-term debt can improve a company's Working Capital
Working Capital depends only on the profit a company generates, and has nothing to do with managing short-term assets and liabilities
practicePrompt.explanation: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. Effective working capital management revolves around optimizing three main levers: how fast inventory sells (DIO), how fast customers pay (DSO), and how long the company takes to pay suppliers (DPO) - these are exactly the components that make up the CCC.

summary.keyIdea: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Cash Conversion Cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: If you run a business or manage family finances, try listing: which items are 'collected slowly' (like receivables), which are 'sitting idle unused' (like inventory), and which 'can be paid later' (like payables)?
application.secondary: Looking at personal cash flow through the working-capital lens helps you see where cash is actually stuck.

sections.text: Working Capital is the cash 'trapped' in day-to-day operations - unsold inventory, money customers haven't paid yet, compared against money owed to suppliers that isn't due yet. Managing working capital well can be the difference between a business surviving and going bankrupt, even while profitable.
The formula and the root cause of being 'cash-trapped'

Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities (short-term assets minus short-term liabilities). Being cash-trapped happens when high Receivables Days (slow customer collection) plus high Inventory Days (goods take a long time to sell) minus Payable Days (time to pay suppliers) produces a large number - meaning the business has to advance cash out for a long time before getting cash back in.
Why fast growth can lead to bankruptcy

Fast growth requires a matching rise in working capital - revenue growing 50% a year usually needs a corresponding increase in raw materials, inventory, and receivables. If the company can't raise enough capital to fund this need in time, it can run out of cash to keep operating even while the P&L still shows a profit - a phenomenon called 'growing broke'. This is a real risk for fast-growing manufacturers, whenever the growth rate outpaces the ability to fund working capital.

items: Ways to free up working capital: collect from customers faster (lower DSO), reduce inventory (JIT inventory), pay suppliers more slowly within acceptable limits (raise DPO)
Amazon has a negative Cash Conversion Cycle - customers pay before Amazon has to pay its suppliers, needing almost no net working capital
A profitable business can still go bankrupt if it fails to manage the working capital demands of fast growth

lines: Profit on paper can't buy raw materials - only cash can do that.
